description: A NASA Space Apps-inspired geospatial time-series dashboard linking historical climate trends to predictive agricultural risks across Southeast Asia.
summary:
Agricultural drought threatens food security across Southeast Asia. Project HEIMDALL is an AI-driven hydro-meteorological forecasting and agricultural drought early warning system built for the Philippines and Southeast Asia. It synthesizes multi-sensor NASA satellite observations, combining FLDAS (NOAHMP001) climate time-series with 1 km MODIS (MOD11A2 v061) Land Surface Temperature statistics.

Using statistical validation alongside a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) deep learning model, the system captures regional rainfall-to-soil moisture coupling (Pearson r = 0.8161) and stationary monsoon cycles (Mann-Kendall p > 0.14). The LSTM achieves high accuracy (R² = 0.9140, RMSE = 0.0217 m³/m³, MAE = 0.0183 m³/m³) in forecasting root-zone soil moisture. Delivered through an interactive web dashboard with a Super El Niño 30-Day Stress Simulator, Project HEIMDALL empowers stakeholders to identify agricultural drought hotspots such as Central Luzon and take proactive mitigation measures under extreme climate anomalies.
details:
System Methodology, Data Utilization, and Statistical Validation

Drought is recognized as one of the most pervasive and prolonged natural hazards, posing severe threats to agricultural productivity, water security, and socio-economic systems. In climate-vulnerable regions such as Southeast Asia (SEA) where local livelihoods heavily depend on seasonal monsoons and agriculture, prolonged water deficits can trigger catastrophic operational and economic impacts. Historical climate anomalies, such as the 2014–2016 super El Niño, demonstrated how severe precipitation deficits rapidly escalate into widespread agricultural drought, affecting more than 50% of regional ecosystems and threatening food security.

Traditional drought monitoring systems have historically relied on sparse ground-based meteorological stations and precipitation-only indicators such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI). However, as established by Hinge et al. (2021) through a comprehensive meta-analysis, while satellite precipitation products (SPPs) offer broad spatial and temporal coverage, standalone meteorological metrics often fail to capture complex sub-monthly variations and are heavily constrained by regional climate types and topography. Furthermore, Li et al. (2022) emphasized that precipitation deficits do not translate uniformly into soil moisture shortages due to land-surface resistance, antecedent conditions, and localized hydrological lag effects. Their findings highlight that monitoring root-zone soil moisture provides a direct and far more accurate indicator of agricultural drought stress than precipitation metrics alone.

To bridge these observational gaps, modern methodologies increasingly leverage multi-source remote sensing data fused with artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning. Recent advancements by Trang et al. (2025) demonstrate that integrating multi-sensor satellite imagery with advanced machine learning algorithms significantly enhances the precision, automation, and spatial resolution of drought risk assessment. Building directly upon these established frameworks, Project HEIMDALL advances regional early warning capabilities by combining multi-variable NASA reanalysis datasets with deep learning (LSTM) architectures.

Data Acquisition, Dual-Platform Utilization, and the 3-Year Window

To capture comprehensive hydro-meteorological and thermal dynamics, this project utilizes two complementary NASA Earth observation architectures across a targeted three-year temporal window (2023–2026).

  • NASA Giovanni (FLDAS NOAHMP001): Extracted area-averaged time-series data covering precipitation flux, surface air temperature, and root-zone soil moisture (0–10 cm).
  • NASA AppEEARS (MODIS MOD11A2 v061): Procured high-resolution (1 km) daytime and nighttime Land Surface Temperature (LST) statistics using a custom boundary polygon over the Philippines.

Why a 3-Year Data Window is Sufficient and Effective?

While multi-decade datasets are great for tracking long-term climate change, a focused 3-year high-frequency window (2023–2026) is ideal for capturing immediate, cyclical shifts like monsoons and El Niño events. Tracking daily data over this localized period gives our AI model plenty of data points to learn from. More importantly, it keeps the focus on recent drought shocks without diluting the signals with outdated climate patterns from the distant past.

Why I Chose These Specific Variables (Giovanni & MODIS)?

To accurately monitor and predict agricultural drought, looking at rainfall alone is not enough a drop in rain does not immediately mean crops are dying, as soil retains moisture for a time. Therefore, I selected a complementary set of variables across two NASA platforms.

  • From NASA Giovanni (FLDAS NOAHMP001): I extracted Precipitation Flux (water supply), Surface Air Temperature (atmospheric heat), and Root-Zone Soil Moisture (0–10 cm) (actual water available to crop roots). Together, these measure the physical cause-and-effect cycle of moisture entering and leaving the ground.
  • From NASA AppEEARS (MODIS MOD11A2 v061): I extracted 1-km Land Surface Temperature (LST) to capture high-resolution, localized ground heat stress across specific agricultural zones in the Philippines.

Figure 1. Precipitation Flux

Displays distinct, high-intensity rainfall spikes concentrated between May and October, corresponding to the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat), contrasted against prolonged near-zero precipitation baselines during the dry months (January–April).

Figure 2. Root-Zone Soil Moisture

Demonstrates a clear hydrological lag response to rainfall inputs. Following the onset of monsoon rains, volumetric soil moisture rapidly saturates at approximately 0.35 m3/ m3 before undergoing a gradual, steady depletion curve down to roughly 0.14 m3/ m3 during peak dry periods visually confirming the antecedent soil memory dynamics required for LSTM sequence modeling.

Figure 3. Surface Air Temperature

Exhibits a consistent annual thermal oscillation, peaking above 300 K (approx. 27°C–29°C) during the pre-monsoon summer months (March–May) which accelerates soil moisture dry-down and cooling toward 287 K (approx. 14°C–15°C regional average) during the Northeast Monsoon (Amihan).

Figure 4: Descriptive Statistics

Before training my AI model, we analyzed 1,399 daily climate records (2023–2026) from NASA FLDAS. We used four statistical methods to verify that our data is reliable and that our chosen climate variables are physically connected.

I utilize descriptive statistics to see the average values, spread, and extreme highs or lows of our climate data.

  • Rainfall: Averages 0.0001 kg/m²/s, with a peak of 0.0005 during heavy monsoon rains
  • Soil Moisture (0–10 cm): Averages 0.2684 m³/m³, dropping as low as 0.1298 during the peak dry season (April 2025) and reaching up to 0.3750 during the wet season (July 2025).
  • Air Temperature: Averages 294.81 K (approx. 21.7°C), ranging from a cool 286.51 K in January to a hot 302.31 K (approx. 29.2°C) in May

Figure 5: Pearson Correlation Matrix

I used the Pearson Correlation Matrix to check if my chosen NASA variables have a direct physical connection. My results show a very strong positive correlation (r = 0.8161) between rainfall and root-zone soil moisture, proving that rain reliably replenishes ground water. Meanwhile, air temperature showed a weaker direct link (r = 0.2840), indicating that heat dries out the soil gradually over time rather than instantly.

Figure 6 and 7: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Regression

I applied Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Regression to test if my climate data follows a simple straight-line trend over time. The analysis yielded very low R-squared (R²) values (0.0022 to 0.0488) and high p-values (p > 0.14) across all variables. From this, I concluded that the regional climate is not driven by a constant upward or downward linear trend, but is instead predominantly cyclic fluctuating in repeating wet and dry seasonal waves.

Figure 8: Mann-Kendall Trend Test

I used the Mann-Kendall Trend Test and Sen’s Slope to double-check for any long-term upward or downward drift without letting extreme monsoon rain spikes distort the results. All three variables Rainfall (p = 0.3342), Soil Moisture (p = 0.1448), and Air Temperature (p = 0.7475) returned a "no trend" result with near-zero Sen's slopes. From this, I concluded that my 3-year dataset is statistically stationary, confirming that the climate shifts are driven by natural, repeating seasonal cycles rather than erratic long-term drift, making the data reliable for training my LSTM model.

What and Where is Changing?

Across this tropical agricultural region, root-zone soil moisture, rainfall, and surface temperature fluctuate strongly together confirmed by a high positive Pearson correlation (r = 0.8161) between rainfall and soil moisture.

How Much is it Changing?

Both parametric (OLS Regression) and non-parametric (Sen’s Slope) analyses show near-zero rates of linear change over the three-year period.

Are These Changes Statistically Significant?

 Using the Mann-Kendall Trend Test and OLS significance testing, all variables returned a "no trend" result with high p-values (p = 0.3342 for rainfall, p = 0.1448 for soil moisture, and p = 0.7475 for air temperature). Rather than indicating a permanent upward or downward climate drift, this proves that the region's changes are driven by stationary, repeating wet-and-dry monsoon cycles confirming why non-linear deep learning (LSTM) is required to accurately forecast agricultural drought shocks rather than simple linear trendlines.

Project HEIMDALL Web Application

Figure 9: Project Heimdall Dashboard

To make my research accessible and actionable, I built the Project HEIMDALL web dashboard an interactive, AI-driven early warning tool for monitoring agricultural drought across Southeast Asia and the Philippines. Powered by a custom-trained Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) deep learning model, the system tracks historical NASA satellite observations alongside predicted and simulated 30-day soil moisture trajectories. The LSTM model achieved strong predictive accuracy, explaining 91.4% of data variance (R² = 0.9140) with minimal error (RMSE = 0.0217 m³/m³ and MAE = 0.0183 m³/m³).

Figure 10. End-to-End Software Architecture

Shows how raw satellite data from NASA is processed and turned into a web dashboard to utilize and visualize the data. It flows through three main steps, collecting climate data, running AI predictions and statistical checks using FastAPI, and displaying interactive 30-day drought forecasts and stress simulators on the user's screen.

Tech Stack

  • Deep Learning & Data Science: Python, TensorFlow/Keras (LSTM neural network), Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and Statsmodels.
  • Frontend & Interactive Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Chart.js (for time-series forecasting curves), and Leaflet.js (for geospatial mapping).
  • Data Sources & Architecture: NASA Giovanni (FLDAS NOAHMP001) and NASA AppEEARS (MODIS MOD11A2 v061), deployed in a resilient Standalone Mode with pre-loaded validation metrics for instant browser performance.

Key Dashboard Features

  • 30-Day LSTM Soil Moisture Forecast: Displays actual historical observations alongside predicted 30-day soil moisture curves and 95% confidence intervals.
  • Super El Niño 30-Day Stress Simulator: Allows users to adjust rainfall anomaly sliders (such as a -40% El Niño drop) to simulate how extreme weather shocks impact future soil moisture
  • Adjustable 30-Day Forecast Schedule: Provides an interactive table where users can manually edit daily projected soil moisture values to test custom scenarios and view real-time risk status updates
  • PH Agricultural Hotspots & LST Map: An interactive Leaflet map highlighting key agricultural zones in the Philippines with clickable alerts based on MODIS Land Surface Temperature (LST) data.
  • Custom Historical Trend Window: Lets users filter and inspect NASA FLDAS variables across specific timeframes (2024, 2025, 2026 YTD, or the full 2023–2026 dataset).

LSTM Machine Learning Approach

To forecast agricultural drought accurately, I designed a custom Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network structured around a clear Input-Process-Output pipeline.

Input (Data Preparation & Sliding Window): I merged the daily NASA FLDAS datasets (2023–2026) for Air Temperature, Rainfall, and Root-Zone Soil Moisture (0–10 cm) into a single clean timeline. I normalized all values between 0 and 1 using MinMax scaling so the neural network could process different measurement units fairly. To teach the model how past weather affects future ground conditions, I structured the data into a 30-day sliding window feeding the past 30 consecutive days of temperature, rain, and moisture into the model to predict the next day's soil moisture. I split the dataset chronologically into 2/3 for training and 1/3 for testing

Process (Model Architecture & Training): I built a sequential deep learning architecture featuring two stacked LSTM layers (64 units followed by 32 units) paired with 20% Dropout layers to prevent overfitting, feeding into a 16-neuron ReLU Dense layer. I trained the model for 35 epochs using the Adam optimizer and Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss, setting a fixed random seed (42) to ensure full reproducibility.

Output (Forecasting & Rescaling): The final Dense output layer generates a continuous soil moisture prediction, which is inverse-transformed back into real-world volumetric units (m³/m³) to produce actionable 30-day forecasts.

Figure 11. Project HEIMDALL

LSTM Soil Moisture Forecasting (Test Set - 1/3 Split): Compares actual observed soil moisture against the LSTM model's predictions on unseen test data, demonstrating close tracking across seasonal dry-downs and monsoon recoveries

Figure 12. Model Training & Validation Loss History

Shows Mean Squared Error (MSE) decreasing rapidly within the first 5 epochs and remaining stable across all 35 training epochs, confirming strong generalization without overfitting.

Figure 13. Parity Plot (Actual vs. Predicted Soil Moisture)

 Illustrates the alignment between actual and predicted soil moisture values against the 1:1 ideal fit line, highlighting high precision particularly during low-moisture drought conditions.

Figure 14. Performance Metrics

On the unseen 1/3 testing dataset, the model achieved strong predictive accuracy with an R-squared (R²) score of 0.9140 (explaining 91.4% of soil moisture variance), a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 0.0217 m³/m³, and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0183 m³/m³.

How This Connects to My Statistical Results?

My earlier statistical tests directly explain why this LSTM architecture succeeded where traditional linear models fail. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression yielded near-zero R² scores (0.0022 to 0.0488) because regional weather moves in repeating seasonal waves rather than straight lines. Meanwhile, the Mann-Kendall test confirmed the climate data is stationary ("no trend"), and Pearson correlation proved strong rainfall-soil coupling (r = 0.8161) alongside delayed heat evaporation effects. Because an LSTM network is specifically built to retain "memory" over a 30-day window, it successfully captured the stationary monsoon cycles and hydrological lag that linear regression missed jumping predictive accuracy from less than 5% (OLS) to 91.4% (LSTM).

Impact of Project HEIMDALL

By translating raw satellite measurements into clear, 30-day predictive simulations, Project HEIMDALL shifts agricultural drought response from reactive disaster relief to proactive planning. It empowers farmers, local government units, and researchers to visualize how upcoming rainfall deficits and heatwaves will dry out crop root zones weeks in advance helping protect harvests, optimize irrigation schedules, and strengthen food security against severe climate events like Super El Niño.

 

Conclusion

Through Project HEIMDALL, I demonstrated how combining rigorous statistical validation with deep learning transforms raw NASA Earth observation data into an actionable early warning system for agricultural drought. By analyzing 1,399 daily records from NASA FLDAS and MODIS across Southeast Asia and the Philippines (2023–2026), my statistical tests revealed that regional rainfall, air temperature, and root-zone soil moisture are strongly coupled (with rainfall and soil moisture sharing a correlation of r = 0.8161) and follow stationary, repeating monsoon cycles rather than simple straight-line trends. Because traditional linear regression failed to capture these non-linear seasonal waves (yielding R² scores below 0.05), I engineered a custom Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network capable of learning 30-day temporal dependencies. This model successfully boosted predictive accuracy to 91.4% (R² = 0.9140) with minimal error (RMSE = 0.0217 m³/m³), proving exceptionally reliable during critical soil dry-down periods. Finally, by deploying these forecasts into an interactive web dashboard featuring a Super El Niño stress simulator and adjustable 30-day risk schedules, Project HEIMDALL bridges the gap between complex satellite science and practical decision-making empowering farmers, researchers, and local planners to anticipate drought shocks weeks in advance and protect regional food security.

Key Findings & Seasonal Outlook (2023–2026 Analysis)

Statistical validation of the NASA FLDAS dataset (January 1, 2023 – October 30, 2026) confirms no significant long-term linear trend across rainfall, air temperature, or root-zone soil moisture. Instead, regional hydro-meteorological dynamics follow a highly predictable, repeating annual cycle driven by the Southwest (Habagat) and Northeast (Amihan) monsoons.

Following the historical seasonal curve from 2023 to 2026, root-zone soil moisture consistently peaks during the mid-year monsoon months before entering a steady depletion phase starting in November and reaching critical lows between February and April. Based on this established cyclic pattern, soil moisture is projected to decline significantly over the coming months, increasing regional vulnerability to agricultural drought.

While seasonal dry-down is a natural annual occurrence, a developing El Niño event in the Pacific threatens to suppress normal rainfall replenishment and elevate surface temperatures. As demonstrated in Project HEIMDALL’s stress simulations, severe rainfall anomalies will accelerate soil moisture loss well below baseline seasonal lows, making early monitoring and proactive irrigation planning critical for agricultural stakeholders.

Local Setup & Execution Instructions

1. Clone the Repository:

Open your terminal or Git Bash and run the following command to clone the project:

 

git clone [https://github.com/Peninsularizz91/PROJECT-HEIMDALL-NASA-SPACEAPPS.git](https://github.com/Peninsularizz91/PROJECT-HEIMDALL-NASA-SPACEAPPS.git)

 

(Ensure you navigate into the cloned directory: cd PROJECT-HEIMDALL-NASA-SPACEAPPS)

 

2. Verify Required Files in Root Directory

Ensure all FLDAS CSVs, MODIS stats, and model files (.keras, .save) are placed in the root directory.

 

3. Install Python Dependencies

Install all necessary packages listed in the requirements file:

 

pip install -r requirements.txt

 

4. Run the FastAPI Backend

Start the local backend server using Uvicorn:

 

uvicorn app:app --reload --port 8000

 

5. Launch the Web Dashboard

Open index.html in your web browser (or serve it via a live server). The dashboard will automatically connect to the live FastAPI backend and render real-time LSTM predictions and Philippine MODIS thermal hotspots.
